proof:
# Private cap motions with shared original halfspaces

This note gives an exact linear-algebra model for moving full-rank
continuous circuits made from original halfspaces. A shared cap has
one normal and one affine base threshold throughout. Having d private
caps per group permits arbitrary nearby affine section motions if the
projected margins may move and a positive offset repair is allowed on
a finite source. It does **not** permit arbitrary motions with fixed
projected margins. The latter obstruction already occurs in a
five-cap inclusion-minimal cover with n=1,d=2, one repeated cap, and
an actual convex source.

Neither private incidence nor the repair proves a mass decrease,
stationarity, or the OC bound.

## 1. Equal-margin coordinates and exact projected coverage

Let xi=(z,1) in R^(n+1). Each original cap has one affine margin

    L_i(z,x)=u_i.x+c_i.xi,  H_i={L_i>=0},

where u_i is nonzero. A selected group I_g consists of d+1 caps
whose continuous normals form a full-rank positive circuit: they
span R^d, and their unique dependence, normalized to sum one, has
strictly positive coefficients lambda_gi.

There is a unique matrix Q_g of size d by (n+1) and vector f_g
in R^(n+1) such that, for every i in I_g,

    c_i=f_g-Q_g^T u_i.                                      (1)

Consequently q_g(z)=Q_g xi is an affine equal-margin section and
F_g(z)=f_g.xi satisfies

    L_i(z,x)=u_i.(x-q_g(z))+F_g(z),
    F_g(z)=sum_(i in I_g) lambda_gi c_i.xi.                  (2)

To prove existence and uniqueness, the square matrix with rows
(u_i^T,-1) is invertible. Its kernel would give u_i.v=t for all
i; multiplying by the positive normalized dependence gives t=0,
and full continuous rank then gives v=0. Solve separately for
each of the n+1 affine coefficients.

The group covers the **whole** continuous fiber over z exactly when

    F_g(z)>=0.                                              (3)

If (3) holds, the positive weighted sum of all margins is
nonnegative, so at least one margin is nonnegative. If F_g(z)<0,
every margin is negative at x=q_g(z).

At F_g(z)=0 the section is the actual common boundary point of
the group's caps. Off that projected boundary it is an equal-margin
reference point, not a common zero. This distinction is necessary
for oblique groups covering only some base fibers. The coordinates
Q_g,f_g use the displayed raw margins; independent positive cap
rescaling can change these coordinates even though it does not
change the halfspaces.

Positive circuits and continuous rank persist under sufficiently
small perturbations of the normals. This follows either from the
invertible augmented matrix or from continuity of the unique
normalized positive dependence. No integer-normalization assumption
is made: both u_i and the base coefficients c_i may be real.

## 2. Exact shared-original equations

For a cap i occurring in groups G_i, choose one reference group g0.
Equation (1) is consistent across its occurrences if and only if

    (Q_g-Q_g0)^T u_i = f_g-f_g0,  g in G_i minus {g0}.        (4)

Once u_i satisfies these equations, the original coefficient vector
is fixed by c_i=f_g0-Q_g0^T u_i. A private cap has no equations (4);
its normal can be chosen freely near its old value and its base
coefficients are then supplied by (1).

Thus (4), one system per shared original, is a necessary and
sufficient exact description of all circuit representations with
prescribed Q_g,f_g and the same original-cap incidences. Nearby
solutions retain all the positive circuits. Shared occurrences may
not be assigned independent copies of u_i or c_i.

For given differentiable motions dot Q_g,dot f_g, let M_i stack
the matrices (Q_g-Q_g0)^T and let b_i stack

    dot f_g-dot f_g0-(dot Q_g-dot Q_g0)^T u_i.

The complete first-order solvability condition is

    M_i dot u_i=b_i                                         (5)

for each shared i. Equivalently, for every collection of vectors
eta_g in R^(n+1) with

    sum_g (Q_g-Q_g0) eta_g=0,

one must have

    sum_g eta_g.[dot f_g-dot f_g0
                   -(dot Q_g-dot Q_g0)^T u_i]=0.             (6)

These are exactly the cokernel conditions, by finite-dimensional
linear algebra. After solving (5), the unique matching derivative
of the original base coefficients is

    dot c_i=dot f_g0-dot Q_g0^T u_i-Q_g0^T dot u_i.          (7)

The same formula handles private caps with arbitrary dot u_i.
The kernel of (5) has dimension d-rank(M_i), so these are the
remaining shared-normal freedoms. If a unit-normal gauge is
additionally prescribed while retaining these Q,f coordinates,
append u_i dot (dot u_i)=0 to (5); it is an additional constraint, not a
free duplication of the shared normal.

For a *finite* prescribed perturbation, replace M_i,b_i by the
new matrices and the exact right side f'_g-f'_g0 in (4). Solvability
and proximity of u'_i to u_i are the exact requirements. On a
constant-rank neighborhood, compatibility plus an invertible minor
constructs a continuous nearby solution (and a smooth one for
smooth data): keep the nonpivot coordinates at their old values
and solve the independent rows. If M_i has full row rank, every
sufficiently small prescribed change in all Q,f is realizable.

First-order compatibility alone does not imply exact compatibility
of a prescribed path, even if M_i has constant rank. Section 5
gives a zero-derivative prescribed path that fails at second order.
This does not say that its zero tangent vector has no other
integrable realization.

## 3. What r private caps actually buy

First keep every shared original cap, including its continuous and
base coefficients, fixed. Suppose a group has t shared caps and
r=d+1-t private caps.

If t>=1, choose a shared index i0. Prescribed new sections Q'_g
are allowed exactly when

    (u_i-u_i0)^T Q'_g = c_i0-c_i
                      for every shared i in I_g.            (8)

Then f'_g=c_i0+Q'_g^T u_i0; define all private c'_i using (1).
Any small independent changes of the private continuous normals
are also permitted.

The t-1 row differences in (8) are independent, because the
normals of a full positive circuit are affinely independent.
Thus each column of the section motion has exactly

    d-(t-1)=r

degrees of freedom. If t=0, its d section coordinates and its
projected margin are all free. If t=1, equivalently r=d, there is
**no section constraint** in (8), but its projected margin changes
by the shared normal's evaluation on that section motion.

This last consequence distinguishes two different claims:

* Arbitrary nearby Q'_g are compatible with one shared cap per
  group if f'_g is allowed to change as above.
* Arbitrary independent Q'_g with prescribed f'_g are subject to
  (4)--(6) and need not be compatible.

For one shared cap in two groups, M_i has n+1 rows and d columns.
Consequently full freedom in prescribed Q,f requires
rank(M_i)=n+1, in particular n+1<=d. If n>=d, there is always
a nonzero cokernel for these raw equal-margin data. This statement
does not depend on how many additional private caps the groups
have; varying their coefficients cannot change the shared identity.

## 4. Coverage during the motion

Let P be a finite set of relevant integer bases and fix an
assignment g(p) with F_g(p)>=0. Any solution of the representation
equations preserves the selected coverage if

    F'_g(p)>=0 for every assigned (g,p).                    (9)

Strict assigned inequalities persist under small perturbations.
For a one-sided differentiable path at a boundary assignment,
dot F_g(p)>=0 is necessary; strict positivity is sufficient for
small positive times, while equality requires control of higher
orders. A two-sided differentiable feasible path requires
dot F_g(p)=0 at that boundary. For affine paths in f, the weak
first-order inequalities themselves are sufficient one-sidedly.
There may also be alternative covering groups; fixing an assignment
is a sufficient condition, not an assertion that the assignment
must persist in every feasible motion.

If every group has at most one shared cap, arbitrary small section
motions can always be repaired on this finite P. First keep shared
originals fixed and construct all f'_g,c'_i as in Section 3; for
groups without shared caps choose any nearby f'_g. Then choose

    kappa=max(0, max_(assigned g,p) [-F'_g(p)]),

and add kappa to the constant coefficient of **every original
margin**, only once per original. This changes each f'_g by the
same kappa and leaves each Q'_g and every continuous normal
unchanged. It preserves all shared identities and enforces (9).
Moreover kappa tends to zero with the proposed perturbation.

This repair enlarges all caps. It is therefore not a mass-preserving
or cap-decreasing variation. With strict original assignment
margins, kappa=0 for sufficiently small motions. At zero margins,
the maximum formula is generally only Lipschitz; it does not give
a two-sided differentiable path with an arbitrarily prescribed
derivative.

For infinitely many integer bases, small coefficient changes are
not controlled merely by checking finitely many old strict signs.
The following two scoped guarantees suffice:

1. Keeping every f_g exactly fixed preserves the projected cover
   for all real and integer bases without further hypotheses.
2. If the projected closed polyhedron {z:F_g(z)<=0 for all g} is
   bounded, nonempty, and contains no integer point, the cover
   persists for all sufficiently small changes of its affine
   coefficients. Boundedness means its recession system has no
   nonzero direction and is stable under small perturbations.
   The resulting polyhedra lie in one fixed ball; any sequence of
   newly feasible integer points has a constant subsequence, whose
   limit would be an integer point of the old polyhedron. This
   contradicts its assumed integer freeness.

The latter condition deliberately excludes projected boundary
integer contacts. Such contacts can lose coverage under an
arbitrarily small adverse perturbation. No generic stability of
closed mixed covers at their integer contacts is being assumed.

## 5. An exact one-repeat obstruction, already at minimal cover

Take n=1,d=2, and coordinates (z,x,y). There are five original
closed caps. Their two groups have margins

    A:  (x, y-z, -x-y-2z),
    B:  (x, -y+z-1, -x+y+2z-2).                            (10)

Only x is shared. Each group has two private caps, continuous
rank two, and positive dependence (1,1,1). Its representation is

    q_A(z)=(-z,0),    F_A(z)=-z,
    q_B(z)=(z-1,0),   F_B(z)=z-1.                          (11)

Group A covers every fiber z<=0 and group B every fiber z>=1.
Hence these five original caps cover Z times R^2.

They form an inclusion-minimal cover on the actual compact
full-dimensional convex body

    C=[0,1] times [-1/4,1/4]^2.

For epsilon=1/20, the following five actual mixed points belong
strictly to just their indicated cap:

    shared x:       (z,x,y)=(0, epsilon, -epsilon/2),
    private A1:                 (0,-epsilon, 2epsilon),
    private A2:                 (0,-epsilon,-epsilon),
    private B1:                 (1,-epsilon,-2epsilon),
    private B2:                 (1,-epsilon, epsilon).

Every non-own margin is strictly negative. Each witness is in
the interior of its actual fiber, so essentiality also holds on
positive-area subsets. This is neither a duplicated cap nor a
redundant-group example. Here h=2^n=2 and

    N=5=h(d+1)-1.

Now prescribe F'_A=F_A, F'_B=F_B, q'_B=q_B, and
q'_A=q_A+t e_1. Allow all five cap coefficients and normals to
change, but require the one shared cap to remain one original.
Its new continuous normal (a,b) would have to satisfy

    a(1-2z+t)=1-2z for all real z.                         (12)

The coefficient of z gives a=1, and then the constant term forces
t=0. No nonzero prescribed motion is realizable, despite both
groups having d private caps. This is an exact obstruction, not
just a failed first-order choice of normals.

At the original configuration, M has image spanned by (-2,1)
in affine coefficient coordinates (z,1). The proposed first-order
right side is (0,-1), outside this image. Replacing t by t^2
instead gives zero prescribed derivatives at zero and passes
the linearized condition, but (12) still makes the finite motion
impossible for every t!=0. This illustrates the integrability
qualification in Section 2.

If projected margins may change, keeping the shared cap x fixed
does realize q'_A=q_A+t e_1 with F'_A=-z+t. Positive t keeps the
integer cover, while negative t leaves a gap on z=0. For example,
at z=0 and (x,y)=(t,0), all three A margins equal t<0, while both
private B margins remain negative for small |t| and the shared
margin is t<0. A common positive offset repair restores coverage,
at the explicitly stated cost of enlarging caps.

## 6. Exact normal-motion force and its surviving cokernel

The linear algebra gives a concrete admissible cap variation. Keep
all Q_g,f_g fixed. For a shared cap i, every vector v in ker(M_i)
gives the exact finite path

    u_i(t)=u_i+t v,
    c_i(t)=f_g0-Q_g0^T u_i(t).                             (13)

All its group identities remain true exactly, and all other
original caps can be left fixed. For a private cap, v is arbitrary.
For sufficiently small t the circuits stay positive, and every
projected margin is unchanged. Thus this path preserves any
original finite-source or all-integer projected cover.

Suppose now the actual finite source fibers are full-dimensional,
and each trace of this cap is either proper or strictly full/empty.
Use its actual coarea sections

    d tau_z = |u_i|^(-1) d H^(d-1)
                 on K_z intersect {L_i=0},

with zero terms on the strict full/empty fibers. Define

    R_i^g0=sum_z integral (x-q_g0(z)) d tau_z.              (14)

The derivative of the original cap's **full mixed mass** along
(13) is v.R_i^g0. Here is the small extension of the proper-section
differentiation in
candidate cd3cb3fa09220cc8,
Section 2, to a nonzero F_g0. On a fixed fiber, write
x=q+xi_perp+a u/|u| with xi_perp perpendicular to u. The moving
boundary has

    a(t)=-(F+t v.xi_perp)/(|u|+t v.u/|u|).

At its old boundary point, differentiation gives
a'(0)=-v.(x-q)/|u|. Fubini gives the signed swept volume;
properness, boundedness, and the zero measure of the section's
relative boundary justify dominated convergence exactly as in
the cited argument. Strict full/empty traces stay fixed locally.
Summing over the finitely many actual fibers proves the formula,
including the varying base coefficients in (13).
Equivalently, for a general representable motion the derivative is

    dot u_i.R_i^g0
      +sum_z tau_z(K_z)[dot F_g0(z)-u_i.dot q_g0(z)].        (15)

For a shared cap, the same expression results from every occurrence,
because equations (5) and (7) specify a single physical margin.
If g replaces g0 in (14), the difference is

    R_i^g-R_i^g0=-(Q_g-Q_g0) sum_z xi tau_z(K_z),

which lies in range(M_i^T). Consequently the projection of R_i
onto ker(M_i) is independent of the reference group.

If this projected force is nonzero, choose
v=-projection_(ker M_i) R_i. The cap strictly decreases to first
order, all other caps remain unchanged, and coverage is preserved.
Conversely, stationarity under all these normal/base-coefficient
motions requires exactly

    R_i in range(M_i^T).                                  (16)

For a private cap this reduces to R_i=0. For a shared cap it
does not generally force a zero section displacement; its surviving
force is precisely a shared-incidence cokernel force.

This distinction is realized exactly in Section 5's actual source.
For the shared cap x>=0 and reference section q_A(z)=(-z,0),
the two coarea sections have length 1/2 each. Their y moments
vanish, so R_i^A=(1/2,0), not zero. The row space of M is the
x direction and ker M is the y direction. Every allowed motion
of this form is x+t y>=0, which bisects both centered square
fibers exactly. Thus its global mass is stationary (indeed
constant) despite this nonzero reference-section displacement.

If one insists on a unit-continuous-normal gauge while holding
the raw Q,f fixed, restrict (13) infinitesimally to
ker(M_i) intersect u_i-perp. Its stationarity condition is then
R_i in range(M_i^T)+span(u_i). Normalization can alternatively be
performed after constructing the physical cap path, since positive
rescaling changes no halfspace; it may change its raw Q,f coordinates.
These distinctions avoid confusing a radial raw-normal change with
a pure fixed-offset angular rotation.

Supporting faces of positive section measure require one-sided
derivatives and are outside the differentiability hypotheses here.
No local single-fiber section centroid is substituted for the full
sum (14), and no conclusion about simultaneous strict decrease of
all caps follows from (16).

## 7. Consequence for the high-cardinality defect budget

Under the hypotheses of
candidate f8a85d598f5eddb1,
suppose N=h(d+1)-1 and all selected groups are full-rank circuits.
The defect identity forces exactly h groups and one original
shared between precisely two groups; every other cap is private.
Thus all but those two groups allow independent normal/section
motions without shared identities. The remaining coupling is
exactly one system (4), not two independently variable cap copies.

If instead the single defect is a rank deficit, the full-rank
theory here applies only to the other groups; a rank-deficient
group needs its own relative-space analysis. No full rank is
inferred from the cap count alone.

At n=d=2 and N=11 in the full-rank case, the shared system has
three affine-coefficient equations for a two-dimensional continuous
normal. At least one compatibility condition survives. Private
counts therefore do not automatically supply all the independent
meeting-section variations that a stationarity argument might
want. The finite-source offset repair supplies feasible motions
but gives no favorable sign for their cap masses.

The exact verifier is
